← Skill Manifest Check

How to write a description that actually triggers

A description that reads clearly to you, who already knows what the skill does, is not the same thing as one that gives an agent enough to match a real request against. Before/after rewrites for the most common reason a skill silently never fires.

The gap: written for a reader who already knows

A description has to work for a reader who has never seen the skill before, because that is the position an agent is in on every single request. A description that summarizes the skill's purpose — what it is for, in the author's own mental model — tends to skip exactly the concrete trigger information a stranger, or an agent, would need.

Too vague: "Handles PDF tasks."
Concrete: "Extracts text, splits, merges, and fills form fields in PDF files. Use when the user asks to read, split, merge, rotate, or fill a PDF, or mentions a .pdf file by name."

Name the situations, not the purpose

Swap "what is this for" language for "when should this fire" language: the actual file types, commands, phrases, or situations that should invoke it. This is the single highest-leverage rewrite, because it is what a matching step actually has surface area to work with.

Too vague: "Formats code."
Concrete: "Formats Python files with black and isort when the user asks to format, lint-fix, or clean up a Python file."

Length: enough for one concrete example, not more

Long enough to state the trigger situation and at least one concrete example phrase or file type; short enough to stay a single focused paragraph. If a description is trying to cover several unrelated capabilities, that is usually a sign the skill itself should split into two, not that the description needs trimming to fit.

Avoiding overlap with a sibling skill

Two skills can both mention "file" and "check" without truly competing for the same request. Two skills that both say "validate a configuration file for errors," with no further distinction, genuinely do. The fix is to narrow each description to what makes it different — the specific file type, the specific kind of check — not to reword either one in a way that still describes the same territory.

Common questions

Why doesn't my skill trigger even though the description sounds right to me?

The most common reason is a description that reads clearly to a human who already knows what the skill does, but gives an agent nothing concrete to match a real request against — no example phrasing, no named triggers, no distinctive vocabulary. A description has to work for a reader who has never seen the skill before, because that is the position the agent is in on every request.

What makes a trigger cue concrete instead of vague?

Naming the actual situations, file types, commands, or phrases that should invoke the skill, rather than describing its internal purpose. "Formats code" is vague; "formats Python files with black and isort when the user asks to format, lint-fix, or clean up a Python file" is concrete, because it gives the agent real surface area to match a request against.

How long should a description be?

Long enough to state the trigger situation and at least one concrete example phrase or file type, short enough to stay a single focused paragraph. A one-line description that is only the skill's name restated ("Handles PDF tasks") is almost always too short to give an agent anything to match; several unrelated capabilities crammed into one description is usually a sign the skill should be split rather than the description trimmed.

How do I know if my description overlaps a sibling skill?

Paste both SKILL.md files into a checker that compares descriptions for shared distinctive vocabulary, not just shared common words. Two skills can both mention "file" and "check" without truly competing; two skills that both say "validate a configuration file for errors" with no further distinction genuinely do compete for the same request, and the fix is to narrow each description to what makes it different, not just reword it.

Skill Manifest Check

Paste a SKILL.md file -- the frontmatter-plus-Markdown format Claude Code and similar agent systems use -- and get every common authoring mistake flagged in seconds: missing or malformed frontmatter, a description too vague to trigger reliably, overlapping triggers between two or more skills, and a body-size caution against a context budget.

Structural pattern-matching, not a trigger test. This tool never runs your skill inside an agent and never calls an LLM to judge it -- it only looks at the text you paste and flags known failure shapes in it. A finding is something worth a look, not a verdict, and a clean result is not a guarantee the skill will trigger correctly.

1. Paste your SKILL.md

Paste one skill to check its frontmatter, description, and body size. Add a second (or more) to also check whether their descriptions overlap enough to compete for the same request. Nothing here is uploaded -- everything runs in this page.

Nothing you paste -- no SKILL.md contents, names, descriptions, or findings -- is ever recorded, uploaded, or sent to an analytics service. Uncheck to turn it off. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control disable counting automatically.

    Common questions

    What does this tool check in a SKILL.md file?

    Four things: the YAML frontmatter has a valid name and description, the description gives an agent enough to trigger reliably (length, a concrete trigger cue, and real distinctive vocabulary), whether two or more pasted skills have descriptions that could compete for the same request, and a rough token estimate for the instruction body against a documented caution line.

    Does this tool contact a network, an AI model, or Anthropic's servers?

    No. Every check is a deterministic pattern match against the text you paste, entirely in your browser. It never calls an LLM to judge the skill, never uploads anything, and never checks whether the skill actually triggers inside a real agent session.

    Is a clean result a guarantee the skill will trigger correctly?

    No. Every check here is a structural, pattern-matching signal against known failure shapes, not a semantic understanding of your description or a real trigger test. A skill with zero findings can still fail to trigger in an actual agent session, and a skill that trips a finding can still work fine -- read every finding as worth a look, not a verdict.

    Why does pasting more than one SKILL.md matter?

    An agent with many skills loaded has to pick one for each request. Two skills whose descriptions share too much distinctive vocabulary compete for the same request even if neither file is wrong on its own -- this tool only checks for that overlap when you paste two or more skills at once.

vs-reading-the-skill-by-hand.html.text:
Skill Manifest Check · comparison

Skill Manifest Check vs. reading the SKILL.md by hand

A careful reviewer genuinely catches a missing field or an obviously short description. This page names no company or product — reading a SKILL.md before publishing it is a habit most skill authors already have, not a competing tool.

What a careful read catches reliably

A missing name or description field, an obviously malformed frontmatter block, a description that is a few words long — those are visible on the page, and a reviewer who knows to look for them catches them the same way this tool's frontmatter checks do.

What gets harder as soon as the judgment isn't about one file alone

CaseReading by handThis tool
A description with no trigger cueCan read as clear, grammatical English while giving a dispatcher nothing concrete to match a real request against -- "clear" and "functions as a trigger" are different judgmentsChecks for an explicit "use when...", an example phrasing, or a quoted sample request, separately from whether the prose reads well
Two skills competing for the same requestThe defect lives in the relationship between two files, not in either one -- requires holding every other skill's exact wording in mind while reading each oneRuns a distinctive-vocabulary overlap check across every pasted skill at once, the same way on every run
An oversized instruction bodyLooks short as rendered on screen; token count and screen length are not the same measurementEstimates tokens from character count and flags against a documented caution line
A description that is long enough but still genericWord count is easy to eyeball; whether the words used are actually distinctive to this skill's job is a slower, easier-to-skip judgmentChecks length and distinctive vocabulary as separate signals, after removing a fixed filler-word list

The gap that matters most: overlap is a property of the whole bundle, not one file

Whether a skill's description competes with a sibling's is not something the file itself can tell you by being read carefully — it depends on what every other skill in the same bundle says, and that comparison gets harder to hold in your head as the bundle grows. A mechanical Jaccard overlap check over the distinctive words in each description does not get tired or skip a pair; it runs the same comparison across all of them every time.

When to still read the skill yourself

This is a structural, pattern-matching scan, not a real trigger test inside an agent runtime. It cannot tell you whether a specific description will actually fire on a specific request, and a skill that trips no finding here can still fail to trigger in practice. Judging whether the skill's instructions are actually correct for the task, and whatever wording this tool's heuristics don't recognise, is still a job for reading the file yourself.

Common questions

What does reading a SKILL.md by hand actually catch?

A reviewer catches a missing frontmatter field, an obviously malformed name, or a description that is simply too short. Those are real defects and a careful read finds them the same way this tool's frontmatter checks do.

Why is a missing trigger cue hard to catch by eye?

A description can read as clear, well-written English to a human and still give an agent's dispatcher nothing concrete to match a real request against. Judging whether a sentence actually functions as a trigger cue -- an explicit "use when...", an example phrasing, a quoted sample request -- is a different read than judging whether the sentence is grammatical, and the two can disagree.

Why is overlap between two skills hard to catch by reading each one alone?

Because the defect isn't in either file -- it's in the relationship between them. Two descriptions can each be well-written on their own and still share enough distinctive vocabulary that a dispatcher choosing between skills for one request could reasonably pick either. Reading skill A and later reading skill B does not surface that unless the reviewer is holding every other skill's exact wording in mind at the same time, across however many skills the bundle has.

Why is a body-size estimate hard to judge by eye?

A skill's instruction body can look short on screen and still run long in tokens once headings, code fences, and examples are counted -- length as rendered and length as consumed by the model are not the same measurement, and a reviewer scrolling the file is judging the first one.

Does a clean result mean the skill will trigger correctly?

No. Every check here is a structural, pattern-matching signal against known failure shapes, not a real trigger test inside an agent runtime. A skill with zero findings can still fail to trigger in practice, and this tool has no way to observe that -- read a clean result as "no known authoring mistake found," not as a guarantee.
